title: Datagram Transport Layer Security Version 1.2
summary: Specifies version 1.2 of Datagram Transport Layer Security, which gives communications privacy for datagram protocols. It is based on TLS and designed to prevent eavesdropping, tampering, and message forgery, while allowing for datagram behavior such as loss and reordering. It was replaced by RFC 9147.

plainLanguage.summary: DTLS 1.2 protects communications sent over datagram transports while preserving the possibility of lost or reordered data. It adapts TLS 1.2 with explicit record numbering and a handshake that can retransmit messages.

questions: how does dtls differ from tls
what is the dtls cookie exchange
subtitle: TLS 1.2 security mechanisms adapted for datagrams that can be lost or reordered.

tldr.problem: TLS assumes a reliable, ordered transport, but some applications send data over datagram transports where packets may be lost or reordered.
tldr.mechanism: DTLS 1.2 adds explicit record sequence numbers and epochs, handshake message sequencing and fragmentation, retransmission timers, and a stateless cookie exchange.
tldr.outcome: RFC 6347 is obsoleted by RFC 9147, which specifies DTLS 1.3.

today: RFC 6347 is a Proposed Standard and was obsoleted by RFC 9147. It was also updated by RFC 7507, RFC 7905, RFC 8996, RFC 9146, and RFC 10015.

sections.title: Security for Datagram Applications
sections.content:
TLS is designed to run over a reliable transport such as TCP. Datagram applications may instead use transports where packets can be lost or arrive in a different order, so TLS cannot be used unchanged.

DTLS is designed to remain as similar to TLS as possible. It protects communications while leaving the delivery behavior of the underlying datagram transport unchanged; it does not retransmit application data.
sections.plainLanguage: DTLS provides TLS-style security to applications that use datagrams. It does not make their data reliable: a lost application packet can remain lost.

sections.title: Handling Loss, Reordering, and Replay
sections.content:
DTLS gives each record an explicit sequence number so a receiver can check it independently of missing records. An epoch identifies the cipher state used for the record. The protocol also prohibits stream ciphers because their state cannot be accessed independently for reordered records.

Handshake messages have sequence numbers and can be queued when received out of order. Large handshake messages can be fragmented across records. Implementations can also use a sliding window to detect replayed records.
sections.plainLanguage: Every record carries its own number, so a missing record does not make later records impossible to check. Handshake messages can be reordered, split into pieces, and retransmitted.

sections.title: The DTLS Record Layer
sections.content:
A DTLS record includes the content type, protocol version, epoch, sequence number, length, and fragment. The epoch changes when the cipher state changes, while sequence numbers are maintained separately within each epoch.

Each record must fit in one datagram, though one datagram may contain multiple records. Applications arrange to distinguish separate DTLS associations because the records do not contain an association identifier.
sections.plainLanguage: A record carries the information needed to identify its content, cipher state, and position. A record cannot span datagrams, though several records can share one datagram.

sections.title: Handshake Cookies and Retransmission
sections.content:
A server may send a HelloVerifyRequest with a cookie after receiving a client's initial ClientHello. The client returns the cookie in another ClientHello. A server can verify the cookie without keeping per-client state, helping it resist requests with forged source addresses.

The handshake assigns sequence numbers to messages, supports fragments, and groups messages into flights for retransmission. A timer triggers retransmission when a response does not arrive.
sections.plainLanguage: The server can ask the client to return a cookie before allocating state for the handshake. If handshake messages are lost, the endpoints can retry a flight of messages.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC identifies denial-of-service risks from repeated handshake requests and from a server sending large replies to a forged address. The cookie exchange helps check that a client can receive packets at the claimed address, but does not stop attacks from valid addresses.

Implementations should generally discard invalid datagrams silently. Sending alerts in response to forged UDP packets can expose a server to denial of service.
sections.plainLanguage: The cookie exchange can reduce attacks that use forged source addresses, but it does not prevent every denial-of-service attack. The RFC advises care when responding to invalid packets.
